title: Conversion
hookLine: study, commitment, and usually immersion in a mikveh

cards: A widow on a dusty road, her mother-in-law telling her to turn back. Go home, the older woman says; your own people are there. Her sister-in-law kisses her and goes.

But Ruth, a Moabite with every reason to leave, holds on. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, she says: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." She walks into Bethlehem a stranger.
The book that carries her name ends with a family tree, and at the end of that tree is King David. Ruth is the story Jews tell about joining.

teach.h: THE DOOR IS NOT PUSHED OPEN.
teach.b: You met Ruth on that road, and the heart of a stranger, in earlier years. Today, how joining actually happens.
It's called giyur, conversion, from ger, which in the Torah means a stranger living among the people; later the rabbis used the same word for someone who joins. The door isn't pushed open.
The Talmud describes a would-be convert being asked, honestly, why they want to join a people that has often suffered, and told about some of the commandments, easy and hard.
If they say, I know, and I am still not worthy, they are accepted. The questions are a kind of respect: this is a real choice.

teach.h: STUDY, AND A COURT OF THREE.
teach.b: Then come study and commitment: time spent learning, living a Jewish year, and in traditional practice, coming before a rabbinic court of three to accept the commandments.
Movements differ on the details and on who may sit on that court.
Usually there is immersion in a mikveh, the ritual pool, and for men, in traditional practice, circumcision, or a symbolic drop of blood if already circumcised.
The person goes into the water and comes up a Jew.
A convert takes a Hebrew name, often as son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. And the past is closed: the Talmud teaches that you must not remind a convert of what they used to be.
The Torah says, "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger." A ger is not a guest. A ger is family.

how: A person converting to Judaism usually studies with a rabbi, appears before a rabbinic court, and immerses in a mikveh; in traditional practice men are also circumcised. The convert takes a Hebrew name, often as son or daughter of Abraham and Sarah. Movements differ on the requirements.

o: joining the Jewish people by study, a court and water
becoming more observant after growing up Jewish
a blessing a stranger gets as a guest at Shabbat

p: a stranger who lives among you

s: a convert can be reminded of their old life
the Talmud teaches that you must not remind a convert of what they used to be.
the would-be convert is told about hard commandments too
the Talmud describes honest questions and both easy and hard commandments.
Ruth's sister-in-law stayed with Naomi too
she kissed Naomi and went home; Ruth was the one who held on.

games.q: you're Ruth. Naomi tells you to go home to your own people. your sister-in-law has already gone. what do you do?
o: hold on and say: your people, my people; your God, my God.
wait on the road for a sign.
games.why: Ruth holds on and goes to Bethlehem, and her book ends with a family tree leading to King David.

practice: Bring to mind someone who joined something you were born into, a family by marriage, a team, a neighborhood, a country, a faith, and notice how long they've been trying to belong.
On each breath out, let go of one way you still treat them as new, and let one small word of welcome form. If you pray, you can pray for someone you know who has chosen a new path.

wordCard.voice: Giyur. Conversion: honest questions, study, the court, the water, and a Hebrew name as a child of Abraham and Sarah. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: conversion, from ger, a stranger who lives among you.

carryVoice: Your line: a new name. Whoever chose to come in is home. I'll be here tomorrow.
